title: LastTake
tagline: Before you wrap the set, know whether you truly have the scene.
inspiration: At the end of a shoot day the evidence needed to judge whether a scene is ready to wrap is scattered: the current script, the shot list, the captured takes, the script supervisor's notes, the camera and sound reports, continuity references, the release ledger. Nobody holds all of it at once, and the failure is discovered too late. While the set is still standing, a missing shot costs about fifteen minutes. Once cast, location and equipment are released, the same missing fact becomes a pickup day, a compromised edit, or a clearance escalation. The cost is asymmetric, and the person who could still act, the script supervisor, is the one with the least time to reconcile it.
what_it_does: LastTake is a second set of eyes for the script supervisor and a safe decision packet for the 1st AD. When a wrap checkpoint fires, four bounded checks reconcile the supplied records: coverage (required beats against captured takes), continuity (preferred takes that would constrain the edit), metadata (slate, media, sound, lens reconciliation) and rights (every person and visible asset traced to a release or licence). A deterministic gate with no model in it combines the findings and either refuses or emits an eligibility result. Two material transitions, the pickup and the wrap, suspend the run with a real Strands interrupt and wait for a named human role; the run resumes later in a different process from the session stored on S3. An approved action publishes one EventBridge event under an idempotency key, and a sealed, versioned turnover goes to editorial with every accepted exception still on it. Absent evidence is a finding, never a pass. The product may not judge creative quality, may not declare anything legally cleared, and may not approve a wrap. Those stay with people, and the interface says so.
how_we_built_it: Strands Agents SDK on AWS Lambda (arm64) behind an API Gateway HTTP API; Aurora DSQL for run state, findings, decisions and handled events, each record sealed with its own SHA-256 and verified before the gate reads a field; S3 for the supplied artifacts (content addressed), the suspended Strands sessions and the turnover manifests; EventBridge for approved actions; a React workspace served as static files from S3 through CloudFront. The public deployment uses an offline lexical interpreter behind the same port that Amazon Bedrock implements, so the demo is reproducible without a model and the model path is not active there. Everything deploys from GitHub Actions; every frontend release names its commit in the HTML, in /release.json and in a public acceptance receipt written only by a pipeline run that walked 26 desktop and mobile browser journeys against the live URL.
challenges: Strands replays a tool body from its first line on resume, so any external effect placed before the interrupt fires twice; every approved action now sits after the interrupt behind an idempotency key, proven in a browser by approving, counting pickup.requested, resending the identical approval and counting again. A model can withhold a pass but must never manufacture one: an ablation that removed the interpreter made the covered count go up (31 to 32), which exposed two fail-open paths, both fixed. Human decisions are bound to the digest of the finding they were taken about, so an approval expires when the evidence moves and the page says which one and why. Twice, a screen shipped that said what a judge would like to read rather than what the system did; both were found by reading the deployed page and removed, and the uptime check now greps the served bundle for such sentences.
accomplishments: Of 34 required beats in the fictional scene, the checkpoint reports 31 covered with evidence, 2 raising exceptions with named sources, and 1 with no release record routed to production (python -m pytest tests/test_corpus_counts.py). The pause-and-resume across process death is exercised on the deployed architecture on every release. A person can supply a take or a release record from the browser, see the findings change, and see a prior approval withdrawn when the evidence it was about moves. Editorial receives a sealed manifest and a portable receipt that carry their own run, policy version and open items.
what_we_learned: Every real defect on this project was found by reading deployed output: a browser test on the live URL, a curl of the API, a grep of the served bundle. Reasoning about the code found none of them. Absent evidence has to be a finding at every layer, including the interface, or a reassuring screen becomes the failure.
what_is_next: Bedrock on the public path once its semantic value over the lexical reader is measured against the frozen cases already prepared (docs/model-evidence-protocol.json); one real production input format with a safe preview; a bounded offline experience for a set with no signal; and the walkthrough by a practising script supervisor that no automated journey replaces.
limits_stated_plainly: The corpus is synthetic: THE LAST FERRY is a fictional production and the packet says so on its face.
No footage or audio is analysed. Sound checks reconcile supplied metadata only.
Nothing is legally cleared by this system; a verified rights row means the expected record was found and its fields matched policy.
No practising script supervisor has run it. Automated journeys are not user validation.
Human active time, interruptions and corrections are unmeasured; timing a model and calling it human time saved would be a fabricated benchmark.
